Warm-Up: Retrieve & Review

1 Classify Structure (LO1)

Classify CH3CH2Br vs (CH3)3CBr as 1°, 2°, or 3°.

Answer Check[ + Reveal ]
CH3CH2Br = Primary (1°) (1 C on α-C)  |  (CH3)3CBr = Tertiary (3°) (3 Cs on α-C)

2 Draw Bond Polarity (LO1)

Draw δ+ / δ− partial charges on C—Br and explain why.

Answer Check[ + Reveal ]
C(δ+)—Br(δ−): Br is more electronegative than C, pulling bonding electrons toward Br.

3 Clean Synthesis (LO2)

Recall one clean synthesis of bromoethane from ethanol.

Answer Check[ + Reveal ]
3 CH3CH2OH + PBr3 → 3 CH3CH2Br + H3PO3 (heat; or KBr + conc. H2SO4 / HBr).

4 Core Definitions (Ch. 14)

Define nucleophile and heterolytic fission.

Answer Check[ + Reveal ]
Nucleophile: electron-pair donor attracted to δ+. Heterolytic fission: one atom keeps both bonding electrons.

Stage 2: Core Concept (LO3) Coursebook Section 16.2 • Crash Course #20 (“Dance Partners”)

Molecular Hotspots & Nucleophilic Attack

1. Nucleophilic Substitution

  • A nucleophile donates an electron pair to a partial positive C(δ+) hotspot.
  • The halogen leaves via heterolytic fission as a halide ion (X−).

2. Follow the Electron Flow

  1. Attract: :OH− approaches C(δ+) opposite Br.
  2. Attack & Break: Lone pair → C(δ+); C—Br pair → Br(δ−).
  3. Substitute: Ethanol forms; :Br− departs.
Turn & Talk: Why does :OH− attack C instead of Br? [ + Reveal ]
Opposite charges attract! Br is δ− (electron-rich, repels :OH−), whereas C is δ+ (electron-deficient).
Fig. 16.2 — Nucleophilic Attack: CH3CH2Br + :OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br−
Step 1: Attraction to C(δ⁺)

The Nucleophile Toolkit with Bromoethane (CH3CH2Br)

Nucleophile Reagent & Conditions Ionic Equation & Product
:OH− NaOH(aq),
heat under reflux		 CH3CH2Br + OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br−
Product: Ethanol (fast hydrolysis)
H2O: Warm water
(ethanol co-solvent)		 CH3CH2Br + H2O → CH3CH2OH + H+ + Br−
Product: Ethanol (slow hydrolysis)
:CN− KCN in ethanol,
heat under reflux		 CH3CH2Br + CN− → CH3CH2CN + Br−
Product: Propanenitrile (+1 C chain!)
:NH3 Excess NH3 in ethanol,
heat under pressure		 CH3CH2Br + NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + HBr
Product: Ethylamine (1° amine)
Rows 1–2 • Turn & Talk: Why is NaOH(aq) faster than pure H2O? [ + Reveal ]
OH− carries a full −1 charge (“playground bully”), whereas neutral H2O only has a partial δ− on O (“patient waiter”).

Row 3 Trap • Count the Cyanide Carbon!

CH3CH2Br (2 C) + CN− (1 C) = 3 C → Propanenitrile (never ethanenitrile). Dissolve KCN in ethanol so OH− won’t compete.

Row 4 Trap • Excess NH3 “Baton-Passing”

Product :NH2CH2CH3 still has a lone pair! Excess NH3 stops it from forming 2°/3° amines; pressure keeps NH3 gas dissolved.

Reflux Apparatus & Hydrolysis Rate Prediction

Real laboratory reflux setup: volatile R—X condenses and returns to the flask

Reflux & Lab Setup Rules (CB Fig. 16.3)

  • Water IN bottom, OUT top: keeps condenser jacket full for efficient cooling.
  • Anti-bumping granules: added before heating for smooth boiling.
  • 50–60 °C water bath: strictly NO open flames (ethanol is flammable).

Stage 3: Practical 16.1 • OBSERVE (POE 2) Coursebook p. 328 • Halide Testing & Acidification Guardrail

Lab Observations: Hydrolysis Rates & AgX Precipitates

50 °C Water Bath Results: 1-iodobutane precipitates fastest (pale yellow AgI)

Observed Precipitate Order

  • Tube 3 (1-iodobutane): Pale yellow AgI(s) — FASTEST
  • Tube 2 (1-bromobutane): Cream AgBr(s) — Moderate
  • Tube 1 (1-chlorobutane): White AgCl(s) — SLOWEST

Roles in the Test Tube

  • Ethanol: mutual co-solvent mixing oily R—X with aqueous AgNO3.
  • Water (H2O): the nucleophile releasing X− ions.
  • Indicator: Ag+(aq) + X−(aq) → AgX(s)
Lab Guardrail: If NaOH(aq) was used, why add dilute HNO3(aq) before AgNO3(aq)? [ + Reveal ]
Leftover OH− forms a brown precipitate of Ag2O(s) that hides the halide colour! Dilute HNO3 neutralises excess OH− (never use HCl).

Stage 3: Practical 16.1 • EXPLAIN (POE 3) Coursebook Table 16.1 • Bond Energies & Activation Energy

Solving the Paradox: Doorbell vs. Padlock

Bond (Table 16.1) Bond Energy / kJ mol−1 Hydrolysis Rate
C—F467 (Strongest)Unreactive / inert
C—Cl346Slow (White AgCl)
C—Br290Moderate (Cream AgBr)
C—I228 (Weakest)Fastest (Pale yellow AgI)
Polarity = The Doorbell
A larger C(δ+)—X(δ−) dipole attracts the nucleophile — it does not decide how fast the bond breaks.
Bond Energy = The Padlock
Bond energy is the padlock that must actually break before substitution finishes!

Weakest C—I (228 kJ mol−1) → lowest Ea → fastest rate.

You Do (Mini-Whiteboard): Ionic equations for 1-iodobutane + OH− & 1-bromopropane + CN− [ + Reveal ]
• CH3CH2CH2CH2I + OH− → CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + I−
• CH3CH2CH2Br + CN− → CH3CH2CH2CN + Br− (butanenitrile, +1 C!)

CB Fig. 16.5 Print Trap: The textbook omits the outer “−” on the transition-state bracket — always write [ ... ]−!
Spot the Error: Why can’t an arrow start on δ+? [ + Reveal ]
Curly arrows track moving electron pairs — C(δ+) is electron-deficient and has no electrons to donate!

Stage 4: Mechanisms • SN1 (3°) & +I Effect Coursebook Figs. 16.6–16.8 • WB Ex 16.2b

SN1 Mechanism & Positive Inductive Stabilisation

Fig. 16.7 — SN1 Mechanism: (CH3)3CBr + :OH− (3° Substrate)
Step 1 (SLOW): C—Br Breaks

1. SN1 = 2 Steps, 1 Slow Species

  • “1” means 1 species in the slow step: Rate = k[(CH3)3CBr].
  • :OH− joins only in fast Step 2.

2. Why 3° Chooses SN1

  • +I Effect: Three methyl groups push electrons toward C+, reducing charge density.
  • Steric Bulk: Methyls block SN2 backside attack. (2° uses both.)
Turn & Talk: Why does 1° use SN2 instead of SN1? [ + Reveal ]
A 1° carbocation (CH3CH2+) has only 1 +I group and is too unstable to form — while its backside is wide open!

Summary, Assigned Practice & Bridge to Elimination

Three Take-Home Pillars

1
Nucleophile Toolkit (LO3): OH− (reflux → alcohol), H2O (slow), ethanolic KCN (+1 C nitrile), excess NH3 (pressure → 1° amine).
2
Bond Energy Rules (LO4): Polarity rings the doorbell, bond energy is the padlock (C—I 228 < C—Br < C—Cl < C—F 467).
03
Pathway Choice (LO5): 1° → SN2 (1 step, 2 species, [ ]−); 3° → SN1 (2 steps, 1 slow species, +I stabilised 3° C+).
Examiner Shield: Lone pair → C(δ⁺) • [ ]⁻ • +1 C in CN⁻ • HNO₃

  • Workbook pp. 142–143: Exam-Style Q1 & Q3 (stretch).
  • Coursebook pp. 329, 332: Questions 1b–e & 2.

3-Question Oral Recap

2. Controls SN2 vs SN1? → +I carbocation stability & sterics
3. Why dilute HNO3 before AgNO3? → Avoid brown Ag2O

Biblical Perspective • Creation, Stewardship & Healing Scriptural Reflection • Genesis 1:31 • 1 Timothy 4:4 • Genesis 50:20

God Created Nothing Bad: Halogenoalkanes in Cancer Therapy

Good Creation (Gen 1:31)  →  Nucleophilic Substitution  →  Redeemed for Healing

1. God Created Nothing Bad

“God saw all that He had made, and it was very good.” — Genesis 1:31  •  “Everything God created is good.” — 1 Timothy 4:4

Polar C(δ+)—Cl(δ−) bonds and reaction laws are intrinsically good designs; harm comes only from human misuse.

2. Nucleophilic Substitution in Cancer Therapy

Anticancer haloalkanes (cyclophosphamide, bendamustine) heal via nucleophilic substitution: DNA’s guanine :N7 lone pair attacks C(δ+)—Cl(δ−), expelling Cl− to cross-link tumour DNA and stop cancer division.

3. Redeemed to Save Lives

“You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good… the saving of many lives.” — Genesis 50:20

WWII nitrogen-mustard chloroalkanes were redirected into the first leukemia & lymphoma cures—turning God’s good chemical laws into instruments of healing.
